claims.text: Post-heating cooling rate controls residual atomic mobility in noble-metal high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles.
Residual atomic mobility determines whether sufficient atomic interdiffusion occurs to produce a homogeneous single-phase solid solution.
Optimizing cooling rate can prevent phase separation, elemental segregation, and excessive coalescence.
The extent of atomic interdiffusion and ordering before final solidification is governed by residual atomic mobility during cooling.
Cooling rate determines the time available for atomic diffusion.
An intermediate cooling rate retains enough atomic mobility to homogenize the nanoparticles into a single-phase solid solution.
Ultra-rapid cooling freezes atomic configurations that lead to elemental segregation and non-equilibrium phases.
Cooling too slowly permits excessive atomic migration that can cause coalescence or secondary-phase formation.
An optimized intermediate cooling rate will produce nanoparticles with a uniform, single-phase solid solution and a controlled crystal structure such as FCC.
Ultra-rapid cooling will produce elemental segregation and multiple phases.
Slow cooling may produce agglomeration or phase transitions.
Direct flash heating followed by uncontrolled rapid cooling typically produces phase-separated nanoparticles with pronounced elemental segregation and irregular morphology.
The proposed cooling-rate mechanism applies to noble-metal high-entropy-alloy systems synthesized under rapid heating and cooling when precursor composition and thermal gradients are controlled.
The optimal cooling rate and width of its processing window may vary with small changes in system parameters.
